parts.title: Part I — Mammalia
parts.description: Warm-blooded vertebrates with hair or fur. Young are typically born live and nourished with milk produced by the mother. The class includes over 6,400 species ranging from bats and whales to primates and hoofed animals.

parts.title: Part II — Aves
parts.description: Feathered, warm-blooded vertebrates descended from theropod dinosaurs. All living birds have beaks, lay hard-shelled eggs, and are endothermic. With around 10,000 species they are the most diverse group of land vertebrates.

parts.title: Part III — Reptilia
parts.description: Cold-blooded amniotes with scales or scutes, occupying every continent except Antarctica. Reptilia as a living group encompasses turtles, lizards, snakes, amphisbaenians, tuatara, and crocodilians — though birds are technically reptiles too under modern phylogenetics. Turtles are among the oldest reptile lineages, their body plan essentially unchanged for over 200 million years.

parts.title: Part IV — Chondrichthyes
parts.description: Fish with skeletons made entirely of cartilage rather than bone. The class includes sharks, rays, and chimaeras — over 1,100 species. Their evolutionary lineage stretches back more than 450 million years, making them among the oldest jawed vertebrates.

parts.title: Part V — Amphibia
parts.description: Cold-blooded vertebrates that metamorphose from water-breathing larvae to air-breathing adults. Amphibians are the first vertebrates to have colonised land, yet most remain tied to fresh water for reproduction. With around 8,000 species they are the most threatened vertebrate class — around 41% of species are at risk of extinction, primarily due to the amphibian chytrid fungus *Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis*, habitat destruction, and climate change.

parts.title: Part VI — Actinopterygii
parts.description: The largest class of vertebrates with over 30,000 species — nearly half of all vertebrate species on Earth. Ray-finned fish are defined by fins supported by bony spines (rays) rather than the fleshy lobed fins of lobe-finned fish. They range from the tiny 8-mm Paedocypris to the 3-metre Atlantic bluefin tuna, and occupy every aquatic habitat from deep ocean trenches to high-altitude glacial lakes. In Sweden, ray-finned fish dominate both marine and freshwater ecosystems.

parts.title: Part VIII — Loricifera
parts.description: Loricifera (from Latin, lorica, corselet (armour) + Latin fero, to carry or bear), also known as corset animals, is a phylum of very small to microscopic marine scalidophoran sediment-dwelling animals with 44 described species and approximately 100 more that have been collected and not yet described. Their sizes range from 100 μm to c.

parts.title: Part XII — Entoprocta
parts.description: Entoprocta (lit. 'inside rectum/anus'), or Kamptozoa , commonly called goblet worms, is a phylum of mostly-sessile aquatic animals, ranging from 0.1 to 7 millimetres (0.004 to 0.3 in) long.

parts.title: Part XVII — Acoela
parts.description: Acoela, or the acoels, is an order of small and simple invertebrates in the subphylum Acoelomorpha of phylum Xenacoelomorpha, a deep-branching bilaterian group of animals, which resemble flatworms. Historically, they were treated as an order of turbellarian flatworms.

parts.title: Part XIX — Insecta
parts.description: The largest class of animals on Earth — over one million described species — with six legs, three body segments (head, thorax, abdomen), and typically two pairs of wings in the adult. Insects have colonised virtually every terrestrial and freshwater habitat. They are the primary pollinators of flowering plants, decomposers of organic matter, and the base of most terrestrial food webs. Insect biomass is declining at alarming rates — estimated losses of 75% in some European regions over 30 years.

parts.title: Part XX — Arachnida
parts.description: The second largest class of arthropods with over 110,000 described species, including spiders, scorpions, mites, ticks, and harvestmen. All arachnids have eight legs, no antennae, and chelicerae instead of mandibles. Scorpions are among the oldest terrestrial animals (Silurian, ~430 Mya); all fluoresce bright blue-green under UV light.

parts.title: Part XXI — Asteroidea
parts.description: Starfish — marine stars with five or more arms radiating from a central disc. Around 1,900 species inhabit every ocean. Most are carnivorous, feeding on molluscs and other invertebrates by everting their stomach through the mouth. Many species can regenerate lost arms, and some can regenerate an entirely new individual from a single severed arm.

parts.title: Part XXII — Echinoidea
parts.description: Globular or flattened echinoderms enclosed in a hard calcareous test covered in moveable spines. Around 1,000 species occupy all ocean depths. Sea urchins are important grazers of algae; their population explosions can devastate kelp forests. Sand dollars are flattened, burrowing urchins with greatly reduced spines.

parts.title: Part XXIII — Holothuroidea
parts.description: Elongated, soft-bodied echinoderms with a leathery skin and reduced endoskeleton — the only echinoderms that feel fleshy rather than spiny. Around 1,700 species crawl across the seafloor worldwide, ingesting sediment and extracting organic matter. Many expel sticky threads (Cuvierian tubules) as defence; some eject internal organs and regenerate them.

parts.title: Part XXIV — Cephalopoda
parts.description: Cephalopods — octopuses, squid, cuttlefish, and nautiluses. The most intelligent invertebrates, with complex brains, camera-like eyes, and jet propulsion. Many can change colour and texture in milliseconds. The class includes the largest invertebrates ever known, with the colossal squid reaching 14 metres.

parts.title: Part XXV — Caudofoveata
parts.description: Caudofoveata is a small class within the phylum Mollusca, also known as Chaetodermomorpha. The class is often combined with Solenogastres and termed Aplacophora, but some studies have cast doubt on the monophyly of this group.

parts.title: Part XXVI — Monoplacophora
parts.description: Monoplacophora , meaning "bearing one plate", is a paraphyletic class of molluscs with a cap-like shell, inhabiting deep sea environments. Extant representatives were not recognized as such until 1952; previously they were known only from the fossil record, and were thought to have become extinct 375 million years ago.

parts.title: Part XXVII — Scaphopoda
parts.description: Scaphopoda (from Ancient Greek σκᾰ́φης (skáphēs) 'boat' and πούς (poús) 'foot') is a class of shelled marine molluscs (invertebrates within the phylum Mollusca), whose members are known as scaphopods and commonly called tusk shells or tooth shells. They have a worldwide distribution and are the only class of exclusively infaunal marine molluscs.

parts.title: Part XXVIII — Polyplacophora
parts.description: Chitons are marine molluscs of varying size in the class Polyplacophora ( POL-ee-plə-KOF-ər-ə), formerly known as Amphineura. About 940 extant and 430 fossil species are recognized.

parts.title: Part XXIX — Bivalvia
parts.description: Bivalvia or bivalves, in previous centuries referred to as the Lamellibranchiata and Pelecypoda, is a class of aquatic molluscs (marine and freshwater) that have laterally compressed soft bodies enclosed by a calcified exoskeleton consisting of a hinged pair of half-shells known as valves. As a group, bivalves have no head and lack some typical molluscan organs such as the radula and the odontophore.

parts.title: Part XXX — Gastropoda
parts.description: Gastropods (previously known as Univalves; class Gastropoda ) are a vast and diverse group of invertebrates within the phylum Mollusca, comprising the animals commonly known as snails and slugs. With an estimated 65,000 to 80,000 living species, they form the second-largest animal class after the insects.

parts.title: Part XXXI — Tentaculata
parts.description: The larger of the two comb jelly classes, characterized by having specialized tentacles (sometimes long, retracting into sheaths, or branching oral tentacles) used to capture prey.

parts.title: Part XXXII — Nuda
parts.description: Comb jellies entirely lacking tentacles or oral lobes at all stages of life, engulfing prey using a large, muscular mouth.

parts.title: Part XXXIII — Cubozoa
parts.description: Box jellyfish — cnidarians with a cube-shaped bell, highly developed eyes with retinas and lenses, and extremely potent venom in their tentacles. Some species, such as Chironex fleckeri, are among the most venomous animals on Earth, capable of causing cardiac arrest in humans within minutes.

parts.title: Part XXXIV — Scyphozoa
parts.description: True jellyfish — free-swimming marine cnidarians with bell-shaped bodies and trailing tentacles, undergoing a complex life cycle alternating between sessile polyp and free-swimming medusa stages. Most species inhabit coastal waters and open oceans worldwide.

parts.title: Part XXXV — Hydrozoa
parts.description: Hydrozoans — a diverse class of cnidarians including hydras, siphonophores (such as the Portuguese man o' war), and many colonial hydroids. They exhibit remarkable morphological diversity, with some species entirely lacking a medusa stage and others forming complex floating colonies.

parts.title: Part XXXVI — Anthozoa
parts.description: Anthozoa is one of the three subphyla of Cnidaria, along with Medusozoa and Endocnidozoa. It includes sessile marine invertebrates and invertebrates of brackish water, such as sea anemones, stony corals, soft corals and sea pens.

parts.title: Part XXXVII — Staurozoa
parts.description: Stalked jellyfish — unusual cnidarians that are neither truly polypoid nor medusoid but possess characteristics of both. They attach to seaweed or rocky substrates via a stalk, with a trumpet-shaped body crowned by eight clusters of short tentacles, resembling a tiny sea anemone atop a stem.

parts.title: Part XXXIX — Micrognathozoa
parts.description: Limnognathia is a genus of microscopic acoelomate freshwater animal that was discovered in Disko Island, Greenland, in 1994. Since then, it has also been found on the Crozet Islands of Antarctica as well as in the British Isles and the Spanish Pyrenees, suggesting a worldwide distribution.

parts.title: Part XL — Gordioida
parts.description: Gordioidea is an order (sometimes placed at superfamily level) of parasitic horsehair worms. Its taxonomy remains uncertain, but appears to be contained in the monotypic class Gordioida and contains about 320 known species.

parts.title: Part XLI — Phascolosomatidea
parts.description:
Phascolosomatidea is a subclass of the class Sipuncula, the peanut worms, containing two orders:-

Aspidosiphonida containing the single family Aspidosiphonidae
Phascolosomatida containing the single family Phascolosomatidae
Their hooks are arranged in regular rings.

parts.title: Part XLII — Sipunculidea
parts.description: Golfingiida, also known as the Golfingiiformes, is an order of peanut worms. The tentacles form a circle around the mouth, while those of the sister taxon, Phascolosomatidea, are only found above the mouth.

parts.title: Part XLIII — Allomalorhagida
parts.description: Allomalorhagida is a class of worms belonging to the phylum Kinorhyncha. The class historically had no orders, and was only divided into families.

parts.title: Part XLIV — Cyclorhagida
parts.description: Cyclorhagida is a class of kinorhynchs, small marine invertebrates that are widespread in mud or sand at all depths as part of the meiobenthos, commonly known as mud dragons.

parts.title: Part XLV — Sagittoidea
parts.description: The Chaetognatha or chaetognaths (meaning bristle-jaws) are a phylum of predatory marine worms that are a major component of plankton worldwide. Commonly known as arrow worms, they are mostly pelagic; however about 20% of the known species are benthic, and can attach to algae and rocks.

parts.title: Part XLVI — Palaeonemertea
parts.description: Palaeonemertea is a class of primitive nemertean worm. It may be para- or polyphyletic, consisting of three to five clades and totalling about 100 species.

parts.title: Part XLVII — Pilidiophora
parts.description: Heteronemertea is a monophyletic order of about 500 species of nemertean worms. It contains genera such as Lineus and Cerebratulus, and includes the largest and most muscular nemerteans.

parts.title: Part XLVIII — Hoplonemertea
parts.description:
Hoplonemertea is a class of ribbon worms. It contains two orders:

Monostilifera
Polystilifera
The proboscis is armed with one or more stylets; intestine straight, mostly with paired lateral diverticula; no posterior ventral sucker.

parts.title: Part XLIX — Arhynchocoela
parts.description: Arhynchonemertes axi is a species of marine nemertean of uncertain placement. It is the only ribbon worm without a rhynchocoel or proboscis.

parts.title: Part LI — Polyplacotomia
parts.description: Polyplacotomia is a class of placozoans, to this date only comprising Polyplacotoma mediterranea. It was established in 2022.

parts.title: Part LIII — Lingulata
parts.description: Lingulata is a class of brachiopods, among the oldest of all brachiopods having existed since the Cambrian period (538.8 million years ago). They are also among the most morphologically conservative of the brachiopods, having lasted from their earliest appearance to the present with very little change in shape.

parts.title: Part LIV — Rhynchonellata
parts.description: The Rhynchonellata is a class of Lower Cambrian to Recent articulate brachiopods that combines orders from within the Rhynchonelliformea (Articulata revised) with well developed pedicle attachment. Shell forms vary from those with wide hinge lines to beaked forms with virtually no hinge line and from generally smooth to strongly plicate.

parts.title: Part LV — Pterobranchia
parts.description: Pterobranchia, members of which are often called pterobranchs, is a class of small worm-shaped animals. They belong to the Hemichordata, and live in secreted tubes on the ocean floor.

parts.title: Part LVII — Eurotatoria
parts.description: Eurotatoria is a superclass of rotifers.

parts.title: Part LVIII — Eoacanthocephala
parts.description: Eoacanthocephala is a class of parasitic worms, within the phylum Acanthocephala. They feed on any aquatic cold-blooded creature such as turtles and fish.

parts.title: Part LIX — Archiacanthocephala
parts.description: Archiacanthocephala is a class within the phylum of Acanthocephala. They are parasitic worms, which attach themselves to the intestinal wall of terrestrial vertebrates, including humans.

parts.title: Part LX — Palaeacanthocephala
parts.description: Palaeacanthocephala ("ancient thornheads") is a class within the phylum Acanthocephala. The adults of these parasitic platyzoans feed mainly on fish, aquatic birds and mammals.

parts.title: Part LXII — Phylactolaemata
parts.description: Phylactolaemata is a class of the phylum Bryozoa whose members live only in freshwater environments. Like all bryozoans, they filter feed by means of an extensible "crown" of ciliated tentacles called a lophophore, and like nearly all bryozoans (the only known exception being Monobryozoon), they live in colonies, each of which consists of clones of the founding member.

parts.title: Part LXIII — Stenolaemata
parts.description: Stenolaemata are a class of exclusively marine bryozoans. Stenolaemates originated and diversified since the early Cambrian.

parts.title: Part LXIV — Gymnolaemata
parts.description: Gymnolaemata are a class of Bryozoans. Gymnolaemata are sessile, mostly marine organisms and grow on the surfaces of rocks, kelp, and in some cases on animals, like fish.

parts.title: Part LXIX — Clitellata
parts.description: The Clitellata are a class of annelid worms, characterized by having a clitellum – the 'collar' that forms a reproductive cocoon during part of their life cycles. The clitellates comprise around 8,000 species.

parts.title: Part LXXI — Cestoda
parts.description: Cestoda is a class of parasitic worms in the flatworm phylum (Platyhelminthes). Most of the species—and the best-known—are those in the subclass Eucestoda; they are ribbon-like worms as adults, commonly known as tapeworms.

parts.title: Part LXXIV — Monogenea
parts.description: Monogeneans, members of the class Monogenea ( MON-ə-JEE-nee-ə), are a group of ectoparasitic flatworms commonly found on the skin, gills, or fins of fish. They have a direct lifecycle and do not require an intermediate host.

parts.title: Part LXXV — Chromadorea
parts.description: The Chromadorea are a class of the roundworm phylum, Nematoda. They contain a single subclass (Chromadoria) and several orders.

parts.title: Part I — Pinopsida
parts.description: Conifers are a group of vascular plants and a subset of gymnosperms. They are primarily perennial, woody trees and shrubs, mostly evergreen with a regular branching pattern, reproducing with male and female cones, usually on the same tree. They are wind-pollinated and the seeds are usually dispersed by the wind. Taxonomically, they make up the division Pinophyta, also known as Coniferae.

parts.title: Part II — Liliopsida
parts.description: Liliopsida Batsch is a botanical name for the class containing the family Liliaceae. It is considered synonymous with the name monocotyledon. Publication of the name is credited to Scopoli : see author citation (botany). This name is formed by replacing the termination -aceae in the name Liliaceae by the termination -opsida.

parts.title: Part III — Magnoliopsida
parts.description: Magnoliopsida is a valid botanical name for a class of flowering plants. By definition the class will include the family Magnoliaceae, but its circumscription can otherwise vary, being more inclusive or less inclusive depending upon the classification system being discussed.

parts.title: Part IV — Cycadopsida
parts.description: Cycads —constituting the division Cycadophyta—are seed plants with a stout, woody cylindrical trunk with a crown of large, hard, stiff, evergreen and usually pinnate (feather-shaped) leaves. The species are dioecious, that is, individual plants of a species are either male or female. Cycads vary in size from having trunks only a few centimeters to several meters tall.

parts.title: Part V — Ginkgoopsida
parts.description: Ginkgoopsida is a proposed class of gymnosperms defined by Sergei V. Meyen in 1984 to encompass Ginkgoales alongside a number of extinct seed plant groups, which he considered to be closely related based on similarities of morphology of pollen, seeds, cuticles, short shoots and leaves.

parts.title: Part VI — Lycopodiopsida
parts.description: Lycopodiopsida is a class of vascular plants also known as lycopsids, lycopods, or lycophytes. Members of the class are also called clubmosses, firmosses, spikemosses and quillworts. They have dichotomously branching stems bearing simple leaves called microphylls and reproduce by means of spores borne in sporangia on the sides of the stems at the bases of the leaves.

parts.title: Part VII — Gnetopsida
parts.description: Gnetidae, commonly known as gnetophytes, is a subclass of gymnosperms within the class Pinopsida. The group was previously considered the distinct class Gnetopsida within the distinct division Gnetophyta.

parts.title: Part VIII — Polypodiopsida
parts.description: Ferns are a group of vascular plants that reproduce via spores and have neither seeds nor flowers. They differ from non-vascular plants by having specialized transport bundles that conduct water and nutrients from and to the roots, as well as life cycles in which the branched sporophyte is the dominant phase.

parts.title: Part IX — Sphagnopsida
parts.description: Sphagnopsida is a class of mosses that includes a single subclass Sphagnidae, with two orders. It is estimated it originated about 465 million years ago, along with Takakia. The order Sphagnales contains four living genera: Ambuchanania, Eosphagnum, and Flatbergium, which counts four species in total, and Sphagnum which contains the rest of the species.

parts.title: Part X — Andreaeopsida
parts.description: Andreaeaceae is a family of mosses which includes two genera, Andreaea, containing about 100 species, and the genus Acroschisma. The Andreaeaceae prefer rocky habitats ranging from tropical to arctic climates, on which they form tufted colonies, typically with reddish to blackish shoots.

parts.title: Part XI — Bryopsida
parts.description: The Bryopsida constitute the largest class of mosses, containing 95% of all moss species. It consists of approximately 11,500 species, common throughout the whole world.

parts.title: Part XII — Andreaeobryopsida
parts.description: Andreaeobryum is a genus of moss with a single species Andreaeobryum macrosporum, endemic to Alaska and western Canada. The genus is placed as a separate family, order and class among the mosses.

parts.title: Part XIII — Takakiopsida
parts.description: Takakia is a genus of two species of mosses known from western North America and central and eastern Asia. The genus is placed as a separate family, order and class among the mosses.

parts.title: Part XIV — Polytrichopsida
parts.description: Polytrichaceae is a common family of mosses. Members of this family tend to be larger than other mosses, with the larger species occurring in particularly moist habitats. The leaves have specialized sheaths at the base and a midrib that bears photosynthetic lamellae on the upper surface.

parts.title: Part XV — Marchantiopsida
parts.description: Marchantiopsida is a class of liverworts within the phylum Marchantiophyta. The species in this class are known as complex thalloid liverworts. The species in this class are widely distributed and can be found worldwide. Complex oil bodies are only found in the gametophyte.

parts.title: Part XVI — Jungermanniopsida
parts.description: Jungermanniopsida is the largest of three classes within the division Marchantiophyta (liverworts).

parts.title: Part XVII — Haplomitriopsida
parts.description: Haplomitriopsida is a class of liverworts comprising fifteen species in three genera. Recent cladistic analyses of nuclear, mitochondrial, and plastid gene sequences place this monophyletic group as the basal sister group to all other liverworts. The group thus provides a unique insight into the early evolution of liverworts in particular and of land plants in general.

parts.title: Part XVIII — Anthocerotopsida
parts.description: Hornworts are a group of non-vascular Embryophytes constituting the division Anthocerotophyta. The common name refers to the elongated horn-like structure, which is the sporophyte.

parts.title: Part XIX — Leiosporocerotopsida
parts.description: Leiosporoceros dussii is the only species in the hornwort genus Leiosporoceros. The species is placed in a separate family, order, and class for being "genetically and morphologically distinct from all other hornwort lineages." Cladistic analysis of genetic data supports a position at the base of the hornwort clade.

parts.title: Part XX — Pedinophyceae
parts.description: Pedinophyceae is a class of green algae in the division Chlorophyta.

parts.title: Part XXI — Pleurastrophyceae
parts.description: The Pleurastrophyceae were a formerly recognized class of green algae, in the division Chlorophyta. It was created by Mattox and Stewart in 1984, containing four genera. More recent classifications tend to split the group. On the one hand, Tetraselmis seems to be a sister to the so-called UTC clade, thus making it part of the (paraphyletic) Prasinophyceae.

parts.title: Part XXII — Ulvophyceae
parts.description: The Ulvophyceae or ulvophytes are a class of green algae, distinguished mainly on the basis of ultrastructural morphology, life cycle and molecular phylogenetic data. The sea lettuce, Ulva, belongs here. Other well-known members include Caulerpa, Codium, Acetabularia, Cladophora, Trentepohlia and Monostroma.

parts.title: Part XXIII — Chlorophyceae
parts.description: The Chlorophyceae, also known as chlorophycean algae, are one of the classes of green algae, within the phylum Chlorophyta. They are a large assemblage of mostly freshwater and terrestrial organisms; many members are important primary producers in the ecosystems they inhabit. Their body plans are diverse and range from single flagellated or non-flagellated cells to colonies or filaments of cells.

parts.title: Part XXIV — Trebouxiophyceae
parts.description: The Trebouxiophyceae, also known as trebouxiophytes, are a class of green algae, in the division Chlorophyta. Members of this class are single-celled, colonial, or multicellular and are found in freshwater, terrestrial or marine habitats worldwide.

parts.title: Part XXV — Prasinophyceae
parts.description: The prasinophytes are a group of unicellular green algae. Prasinophytes mainly include marine planktonic species, as well as some freshwater representatives. The prasinophytes are morphologically diverse, including flagellates with one to eight flagella and non-motile (coccoid) unicells, as well as dormant or cyst stage phycoma.

parts.title: Part XXVI — Nephroselmidophyceae
parts.description: Nephroselmidaceae is a family of green algae, the only family in the order Nephroselmidales and the class Nephrophyceae within the division Chlorophyta.

parts.title: Part XXVII — Mamiellophyceae
parts.description: Mamiellophyceae is a class of green algae in the division Chlorophyta.

parts.title: Part XXVIII — Chloropicophyceae
parts.description: Chloropicophyceae is a class of green algae in the division Chlorophyta that, along with Picocystophyceae, coincides with the traditional "prasinophyte clade VII". Chloropicophyceae has a single order, Chloropicales with a single family, Chloropicaceae.

parts.title: Part XXIX — Picocystophyceae
parts.description: Picocystis is a monotypic genus of green algae, the sole species is Picocystis salinarum. It is placed within its own class, Picocystophyceae in the division Chlorophyta.

parts.title: Part XXX — Palmophyllophyceae
parts.description: The Palmophyllophyceae are a class of green algae consisting of the Palmophyllales and Prasinococcales.

parts.title: Part XXXI — Bangiophyceae
parts.description: Bangiophyceae is a class of red algae that includes the order Bangiales and possibly Goniotrichales. In some classifications it is merged with the Florideophyceae to form the Rhodophyceae. The Bangiophyceae, as defined traditionally, are paraphyletic.

parts.title: Part XXXII — Cyanidiophyceae
parts.description: Cyanidiophyceae is a class of unicellular red algae within subdivision Cyanidiophytina, and contain a single plastid, one to three mitochondria, a nucleus, a vacuole, and floridean starch. Pyrenoids are absent. Most are extremophiles inhabiting acid hot springs with a pH between 0,2 and 4 and temperatures up to 56 °C.

parts.title: Part XXXIII — Compsopogonophyceae
parts.description: Compsopogonophyceae is a class of red algae.

parts.title: Part XXXIV — Florideophyceae
parts.description: Florideophyceae is a class of exclusively multicellular red algae. They were once thought to be the only algae to bear pit connections, but these have since been found in the filamentous stage of the Bangiaceae. They were also thought only to exhibit apical growth, but there are genera known to grow by intercalary growth. Most, but not all, genera have three phases to the life cycle.

parts.title: Part XXXV — Rhodellophyceae
parts.description: Rhodellophyceae is a class of red algae.

parts.title: Part XXXVI — Stylonematophyceae
parts.description: Stylonematophyceae is a class of red algae.

parts.title: Part XXXVII — Porphyridiophyceae
parts.description: Porphyridiophyceae is a class of red algae.

parts.title: Part XXXVIII — Charophyceae
parts.description: Charophyceae is a class of charophyte green algae. AlgaeBase places it in division Charophyta. Extant (living) species are placed in a single order Charales, commonly known as "stoneworts" and "brittleworts". Fossil members of the class may be placed in separate orders, e.g. Sycidiales.

parts.title: Part XXXIX — Klebsormidiophyceae
parts.description: Klebsormidiales is an order of charophyte algae. Until Bierenbroodspot et al.'s phylogeny, it was the only order in the class Klebsormidiophyceae, sister of the Phragmoplastophyta. As of February 2022, AlgaeBase accepted two families in the order:Elakatotrichaceae Hindák Klebsormidiaceae K.D.Stewart & K.R.Mattox

parts.title: Part XL — Mesostigmatophyceae
parts.description: The Mesostigmatophyceae are a class of basal green algae found in freshwater. In a narrow circumscription, the class contains a single genus, Mesostigma. AlgaeBase then places the class within its circumscription of Charophyta. A clade containing Chlorokybus and Spirotaenia may either be added, or treated as a sister, with Chlorokybus placed in a separate class, Chlorokybophyceae.

parts.title: Part XLI — Zygnematophyceae
parts.description: Zygnematophyceae is a class of green algae in the paraphylum streptophyte algae, also referred to as Charophyta, consisting of more than 4000 described species. The Zygnematophyceae are the sister clade of the Embryophyta.

parts.title: Part XLII — Conjugatophyceae
parts.description: Zygnematophyceae is a class of green algae in the paraphylum streptophyte algae, also referred to as Charophyta, consisting of more than 4000 described species. The Zygnematophyceae are the sister clade of the Embryophyta.

parts.title: Part XLIII — Chlorokybophyceae
parts.description: Chlorokybus is a multicellular (sarcinoid) genus of basal green algae or charophyte. It has been classified as the sole member of the family Chlorokybaceae, which is the sole member of the order Chlorokybales, in turn the sole member of the class Chlorokybophyceae. It grows on soil and rock surfaces, and is rare.
